# Causal effects with cross-fitted double machine learning

```{r causal-effects-setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(rmoriebricklayer)
```

`plrcf()` estimates the average effect of a treatment on an outcome when the treated and
the untreated differ in measured ways (confounders). It fits the partially linear model

\[ Y = \theta D + g(X) + \varepsilon, \qquad D = m(X) + v, \]

by the double machine learning recipe of Chernozhukov et al. (2018): the outcome and the
treatment are each predicted from the confounders \(X\) on folds the row was not part of
(cross-fitting), and \(\theta\) is the regression of the outcome residuals on the treatment
residuals (DML2), with a sandwich standard error. When the effect is the same for everyone,
\(\theta\) is the average treatment effect (ATE); otherwise it is a variance-weighted average of
the individual effects. `exprspplr()` bootstraps the same estimator for a continuous
exposure (see the air-pollution vignette). The nuisances \(g\) and \(m\) are ordinary least
squares fits, so \(\theta\) is consistent when they are linear in the columns given; add squares,
interactions or splines as columns where they are not.

## A known effect, recovered

Confounding biases the simple comparison; the cross-fitted estimate removes it. Here the true
effect of `d` on `y` is 2, and `x1` drives both:

```{r causal-effects-sim}
set.seed(42)
n <- 2000
sim <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n))
sim$d <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(1.5 * sim$x1))
sim$y <- 2 * sim$d + 3 * sim$x1 + sim$x2 + rnorm(n)
mean(sim$y[sim$d == 1]) - mean(sim$y[sim$d == 0])   # biased by x1
fit <- plrcf(sim, "y", "d", c("x1", "x2"))
fit$ate
fit$ate + c(-1.96, 1.96) * fit$se
```

## The NSW job-training experiment, and what observational data can recover

LaLonde (1986) took the National Supported Work Demonstration, a randomised job-training
programme of the 1970s, and asked whether the econometric methods of the day could recover its
experimental effect on 1978 earnings when the randomised controls are replaced by a survey
sample (the PSID). Dehejia and Wahba (1999) kept the men with 1974 earnings: 185 treated, 260
randomised controls, and 2,490 PSID-1 comparison men. The three files are on data.rmorie.com
(`rmbl login` once), checked against the SHA-256 the manifest lists:

```{r causal-effects-nsw-load, eval = FALSE}
tr <- dload("nsw_dw/treated")
ct <- dload("nsw_dw/control")
ps <- dload("nsw_dw/psid_controls")
```

Or, without signing in, from Rajeev Dehejia's own pages (whitespace-separated text):

```{r causal-effects-nsw-open, eval = FALSE}
cols <- c("treat", "age", "educ", "black", "hisp", "married", "nodegree", "re74", "re75", "re78")
nber <- function(f) {
  dest <- file.path(tempdir(), f)
  bldl(paste0("https://users.nber.org/~rdehejia/data/", f), dest)
  stats::setNames(utils::read.table(dest), cols)
}
tr <- nber("nswre74_treated.txt")
ct <- nber("nswre74_control.txt")
ps <- nber("psid_controls.txt")
```

The PSID men are older, more often married and earned about nine times as much before the
programme; the randomised controls look like the treated:

| Mean | age | educ | black | married | nodegree | re74 | re75 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Treated | 25.82 | 10.35 | 0.84 | 0.19 | 0.71 | 2,095.57 | 1,532.06 |
| Randomised controls | 25.05 | 10.09 | 0.83 | 0.15 | 0.83 | 2,107.03 | 1,266.91 |
| PSID controls | 34.85 | 12.12 | 0.25 | 0.87 | 0.31 | 19,428.75 | 19,063.34 |

The experimental benchmark, and the same question asked of the observational sample:

```{r causal-effects-nsw-fit, eval = FALSE}
x <- c("age", "educ", "black", "hisp", "married", "nodegree", "re74", "re75")
exp <- rbind(tr, ct)
obs <- rbind(tr, ps)
mean(tr$re78) - mean(ct$re78)                 # the experiment
mean(tr$re78) - mean(ps$re78)                 # treated against the PSID, unadjusted
plrcf(exp, "re78", "treat", x)
plrcf(obs, "re78", "treat", x)
plrcf(obs, "re78", "treat", x, kfol = 10, seed = 2)
```

Run on 15 October 2026 (1982 US dollars of 1978 earnings):

| Sample and estimator | Effect | Standard error | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|---|
| Experiment, difference in means | 1,794.3 | | |
| Experiment, `plrcf()` | 1,695.9 | 680.8 | 361.5 to 3,030.2 |
| Treated vs PSID, difference in means | -15,204.8 | | |
| Treated vs PSID, `plrcf()` | 618.3 | 791.1 | -932.3 to 2,168.9 |
| Treated vs PSID, `plrcf()`, 10 folds, seed 2 | 748.4 | 777.5 | -775.5 to 2,272.3 |

Adjusting for the eight pre-programme covariates turns a fifteen-thousand-dollar penalty into a
small positive effect whose interval covers the experimental one, though it sits well below it
and is far less precise. Two things limit it. The nuisances are linear, so the large earnings
gap is adjusted for only as a straight line; and the overlap is thin: most PSID men earned more
before the programme than almost any treated man, so the comparison rests on the few who look
like them. Dehejia and Wahba show that trimming the comparison group to the region of common
support (on an estimated propensity score) brings the observational estimate close to the
experiment; with `plrcf()`, restrict `obs` to that region before fitting. The cross-fit
split moves the estimate by about a sixth of a standard error, which is why the seed and the
number of folds are arguments.

## Overlap and balance

Two checks belong with every weighting estimate: whether the two groups overlap (each person has a
real chance of either treatment) and whether weighting balances the covariates. On simulated data,
where the true effect is 3:

```{r causal-effects-overlap-balance}
set.seed(7)
n <- 1500
d <- data.frame(age = runif(n, 18, 70), income = rnorm(n))
d$t <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-2 + 0.04 * d$age + 0.5 * d$income))
d$y <- 10 + 3 * d$t + 0.2 * d$age + d$income + rnorm(n)
fit <- aipwcf(d, "y", "t", c("age", "income"), lrn = "ols")
fit
plot(fit)
plot(fit, type = "estimate")
pr <- attr(fit, "propensity")
e <- pmin(pmax(pr$propensity, 0.01), 0.99)
d$ipw <- ifelse(d$t == 1, 1 / e, 1 / (1 - e))
plot(baltab(d, "t", c("age", "income")),
     after = baltab(d, "t", c("age", "income"), w = "ipw"))
```

The groups overlap where both curves have mass; after weighting, both covariates fall below the
0.1 line.

## Indigenous examples

The person-level questions this vignette is about (does a strong sense of belonging go
with better mental health once circumstances are held equal?) need the survey microdata,
which Statistics Canada distributes as a public use file; `aipwcf()` with
`design = svydes(...)` takes its bootstrap weights directly. The published tables
bundled with the package support the group-level questions; for those see
`vignette("applied-analyses")`. A comparison of the published
estimates themselves:

```{r causal-effects-indigenous-causal}
hi <- indiex("health")
x <- hi[hi$period == "2019/2022" & hi$age == "Total, 18 years and over" &
          hi$indicator == "Perceived mental health, very good or excellent", ]
indgap(x, "group", "estimate", "lower", "upper", qual = "quality")[
  , c("group", "estimate", "refest", "difference", "diflo",
      "difup")]
```

Chernozhukov, V., Chetverikov, D., Demirer, M., Duflo, E., Hansen, C., Newey, W. and Robins, J.
(2018). Double/debiased machine learning for treatment and structural parameters. *The
Econometrics Journal* 21(1), C1-C68.

Dehejia, R. H. and Wahba, S. (1999). Causal effects in nonexperimental studies: reevaluating the
evaluation of training programs. *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 94(448),
1053-1062.

LaLonde, R. J. (1986). Evaluating the econometric evaluations of training programs with
experimental data. *American Economic Review* 76(4), 604-620.
